paper_title: Aesthetic Responses to Exact Fractals Driven by Physical Complexity
abstract: Fractals are physically complex due to their repetition of patterns at multiple size scales. Whereas the statistical characteristics of the patterns repeat for fractals found in natural objects, computers can generate patterns that repeat exactly. Are these exact fractals processed differently, visually and aesthetically, than their statistical counterparts? We investigated the human aesthetic response to the complexity of exact fractals by manipulating fractal dimensionality, symmetry, recursion, and the number of segments in the generator. Across two studies, a variety of fractal patterns were visually presented to human participants to determine the typical response to exact fractals. In the first study, we found that preference ratings for exact midpoint displacement fractals can be described by a linear trend with preference increasing as fractal dimension increases. For the majority of individuals, preference increased with dimension. We replicated these results for other exact fractal patterns in a second study. In the second study, we also tested the effects of symmetry and recursion by presenting asymmetric dragon fractals, symmetric dragon fractals, and Sierpinski carpets and Koch snowflakes, which have radial and mirror symmetry. We found a strong interaction among recursion, symmetry and fractal dimension. Specifically, at low levels of recursion, the presence of symmetry was enough to drive high preference ratings for patterns with moderate to high levels of fractal dimension. Most individuals required a much higher level of recursion to recover this level of preference in a pattern that lacked mirror or radial symmetry, while others were less discriminating. This suggests that exact fractals are processed differently than their statistical counterparts. We propose a set of four factors that influence complexity and preference judgments in fractals that may extend to other patterns: fractal dimension, recursion, symmetry and the number of segments in a pattern. Conceptualizations such as Berlyne's and Redies' theories of aesthetics also provide a suitable framework for interpretation of our data with respect to the individual differences that we detect. Future studies that incorporate physiological methods to measure the human aesthetic response to exact fractal patterns would further elucidate our responses to such timeless patterns.
methodology:
Two behavioral studies were conducted. Participants viewed fractal patterns on a computer screen and rated their visual appeal on a 7-point scale (1=very low, 7=very high). Stimuli were presented for 3 seconds, followed by a 3-second response window. Image presentation order was randomized. 

**Experiment 1:**
*   **Stimuli:** Exact midpoint displacement fractals (generated using Fournier et al., 1982 algorithm), 10 levels of recursion, 1025x1025 pixel binary images (black/white). 
*   **Design:** Repeated measures ANOVA with 9 levels of fractal dimension (D=1.1 to 1.9). Recursion and symmetry were held constant.

**Experiment 2:**
*   **Stimuli:** Four fractal generator rules: Sierpinski carpets (4 recursions, radial & mirror symmetry), Symmetric dragon fractals (10 recursions, radial symmetry only), Golden dragon fractals (10 & 17 recursions, no spatial symmetry), and Koch snowflake fractals (5 & 6 recursions, radial & mirror symmetry). All varied in fractal dimension (D=1.1 to 1.9).
*   **Design:** Repeated measures ANOVA for each fractal set, and a three-way ANOVA for line fractals (Golden Dragon & Koch Snowflake) with factors of spatial symmetry (absent/present), recursion (low/high), and fractal dimension (9 levels). Cluster analysis was used to identify subgroups with different preference patterns in both experiments.
manipulated_features: Recursion (number of iterations: 4, 5, 6, 10, 17 levels depending on fractal type)
Spatial symmetry (mirror symmetry: present/absent; radial symmetry: present/absent)
Generator rule (Midpoint displacement, Sierpinski carpet, Symmetric dragon, Golden dragon, Koch snowflake)
Number of segments in the generator
outcomes: Preference ratings (7-point scale for visual appeal)
key_findings: Overall, preference for exact midpoint displacement fractals increased with fractal dimension (D) and stabilized at high D [F(1.30, 51.92) = 21.71, p < 0.001, η² = 0.35; significant linear (p < 0.001, η² = 0.38) and cubic (p < 0.001, η² = 0.34) trends].

Subgroup analysis revealed two distinct groups: a minority (24%) preferred lower D fractals (preference decreased as D increased), while the majority (76%) preferred higher D fractals (preference increased as D increased) [interaction between D and group: F(2.52, 87.81) = 79.81, p < 0.001, η² = 0.67].

**Sierpinski Carpets (Radial & Mirror Symmetry):** Preference increased linearly with D [F(2.25, 38.30) = 18.77, p < 0.001, η² = 0.53; significant linear trend (p < 0.001, η² = 0.66)]. Subgroups also showed increasing preference with D [no significant interaction between D and group: F(2.20, 35.21) = 9.94, p = 0.73, η² = 0.02].

**Symmetric Dragon Fractals (Radial Symmetry Only):** Preference increased with D to a point, then stabilized [F(2.61, 44.39) = 6.86, p = 0.001, η² = 0.29; significant linear (p = 0.01, η² = 0.33), quadratic (p = 0.009, η² = 0.34), 5th (p = 0.02, η² = 0.29) and 7th (p < 0.001, η² = 0.53) order trends]. Subgroups also showed increasing preference with D [no significant interaction between D and group: F(2.49, 39.80) = 1.47, p = 0.24, η² = 0.08].
**Line Fractals (Golden Dragon & Koch Snowflake - Varying Symmetry & Recursion):**
Main effect of recursion: Higher recursion levels were preferred (M=4.7) over fewer recursions (M=3.59) [F(1, 17) = 94.15, p = 0.001, η² = 0.85].
Main effect of symmetry: Koch snowflakes (mirror & radial symmetry, M=4.68) were preferred over dragon fractals (no spatial symmetry, M=3.61) [F(1, 17) = 17.92, p = 0.001, η² = 0.51].
Main effect of D: Preference showed significant linear and quadratic trends [F(1.76, 29.99) = 25.87, p < 0.001, η² = 0.60; linear (p < 0.001, η² = 0.60) and quadratic (p < 0.001, η² = 0.84)].

Significant three-way interaction among D, recursion, and symmetry [F(3.81, 64.82) = 11.58, p < 0.001, η² = 0.41]. Koch snowflakes (5 & 6 recursions) were rated equivalently across D. Golden dragon (10 recursions) had low, constant preference, while golden dragon (17 recursions) had higher preference that increased with D.

At low levels of recursion, the presence of symmetry drove high preference for patterns with moderate to high D. Most individuals required much higher recursion to achieve this preference level in patterns lacking mirror or radial symmetry.

**Effect of Symmetry in Dragon Fractals (Golden vs. Symmetric):** Radially symmetric dragon fractals (M=3.16) were preferred over golden dragon fractals (no radial symmetry, M=2.54) [F(1, 17) = 23.14, p < 0.001, η² = 0.58].
Interaction between symmetry and D: Preference for radially symmetric dragons increased more with D than for golden dragons [F(3.16, 53.76) = 2.82, p = 0.045, η² = 0.14].

Subgroup analysis for mirror symmetry: The majority subgroup (67%) rated mirror-symmetric fractals much higher than non-mirror symmetric fractals [interaction between mirror symmetry and subgroup membership: F(1, 16) = 37.82, p < 0.001, η² = 0.70]. The minority subgroup (33%) showed no difference in preference based on mirror symmetry.
Overall, exact fractals show a preference for higher D, contrasting with previous findings for statistical fractals (which peak at low-to-moderate D).
theories_referenced: Birkhoff's (1933) theory of aesthetic value (ratio of order and complexity)
Eysenck's (1941) multiplicative relationship for aesthetic value (order x complexity)
Attneave's (1954, 1957) work on perceived complexity (number of line segments, symmetry)
Berlyne's (1971) theory of aesthetics (interestingness, pleasantness, physical complexity, numerosity, symmetry, randomization, arousal model)
Leeuwenberg's (1971, 1978) and van der Helm's (1991, 2004) coding theories (redundancy, load, unique elements, repetitions, transformations)
Redies' (2015) theory of aesthetics (universal beauty, cultural context, cognitive and cultural factors)
Leder et al.'s (2004) model of aesthetic appreciation (balance interest and comprehensibility)
mechanisms: Aesthetics for exact fractals are driven by physical complexity, influenced by four factors: fractal dimension, number of elements in the generator, recursion, and symmetry.
Fractal dimension quantifies the relative contributions of coarse and fine scale patterns; higher D indicates more fine structure.
Number of elements in the generator describes how many elements are introduced at each recursion.
Recursion describes the extent of pattern repetition across scales.
Symmetry describes order at the level of the overall pattern.
Order acts as a moderating factor, preserving interpretability at higher D levels.
Recursion can compensate for a lack of spatial symmetry and drive preference upward at peak D levels by increasing perceived complexity without affecting perceived regularity.
Symmetry in geometric patterns balances interest and comprehensibility, contributing to visual appeal.
Mirror symmetry has evolutionary roots and affects brain responses, suggesting a neural basis for its perception.
Higher D exact fractals may be more engaging than lower D counterparts, leading to higher aesthetic ratings.
limitations: Experiment 1 only presented one fractal pattern at a particular level of recursion, limiting generalizability.
The sample size for Experiment 2 (18 participants) was small, potentially limiting the detection of some subgroup differences.
Insufficient demographic data was collected to test predictions about cultural filters or individual differences in aesthetic responses.
The study did not use a within-subject design to directly compare statistical and exact fractals.
The introduction of a broader array of fractal generators in Experiment 2 might have inadvertently made mirror symmetry a more salient factor.
Leeuwenberg and van der Helm's coding theories, while referenced, have limited scope and do not fully explain the observed interactions between abstracted code and physical units.
design_implications: Exact fractals, with their precise repetition of patterns, offer a new avenue for studying aesthetic responses in built environments and art.
Designers can leverage fractal dimension, recursion, and symmetry to influence aesthetic preference.
For patterns with low recursion, incorporating symmetry can significantly enhance visual appeal, especially for moderate to high fractal dimensions.
In the absence of mirror or radial symmetry, a much higher level of recursion may be needed to achieve similar levels of preference for most individuals.
Patterns that are symmetric in multiple ways and tend to fill more space are generally perceived as more pleasing.

The findings suggest that the 'physical complexity' of exact fractals, as defined by these factors, is a key driver of aesthetic response, which could inform the design of visually engaging spaces and objects.

environmental_features: Fractal dimensions ranging from approximately 1.0 to 2.0
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Participants viewed each fractal image for an unconstrained duration until they provided their ratings.
control_conditions: Different fractal dimensions (D values) served as comparison conditions

theory_commitments.theory_name: Information Theory of Aesthetics / Optimal Arousal Theory
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Aesthetic preference for stimuli is maximized at an intermediate level of complexity or information content, often resulting in an inverted U-shaped relationship.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates how the physical fractal dimension of stimuli influences perceived complexity, which in turn affects aesthetic preference.

instruments_used.name: Aesthetic Preference Scale
instruments_used.description: Self-report rating scale (e.g., 1-7 Likert scale) for how much participants liked or preferred each image.

instruments_used.name: Perceived Complexity Scale
instruments_used.description: Self-report rating scale (e.g., 1-7 Likert scale) for how complex participants found each image.

instruments_used.name: Perceived Pleasantness Scale
instruments_used.description: Self-report rating scale (e.g., 1-7 Likert scale) for how pleasant participants found each image.

stimulus_images.description: Examples of the exact fractal images used as stimuli, illustrating different fractal types and variations in fractal dimension.
